name: Type 2 diabetes (adult)
theme: protect organs early, not just lower sugar

meta.title: Type 2 diabetes teaching guide
meta.population: Adults; screening and prediabetes through newly diagnosed, established cardio-kidney disease, and intensification
meta.summary: Evidence-linked teaching guide showing how adult type 2 diabetes care moves from screening and diagnosis to lifestyle, early organ-protective medicines (SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1-based therapy), intensification including insulin, and lifelong complication checks. Built on the ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026 and the ADA/EASD 2026 consensus report. Every claim maps to a listed source.
meta.disclaimer: Teaching guide. Not medical advice. Your own care team decides.
meta.classification: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Sec. 2 (A1C ≥6.5%, FPG ≥126 mg/dL, 2-h OGTT ≥200 mg/dL, or random ≥200 mg/dL with symptoms; confirm unless unequivocal)
meta.response: A1C (goal <7% for many adults) and/or CGM metrics — time in range >70%, time <70 mg/dL <4%, time <54 mg/dL <1% (ADA 2026 Sec. 6)

stages.label: Screening
stages.question: Should this adult be tested?
stages.decision: Screen at 35+ or earlier with overweight/obesity plus a risk factor; repeat at least every 3 years if normal

stages.label: Diagnosis
stages.question: Is it diabetes, prediabetes, or something else?
stages.decision: Confirm with a second test and consider type 1 features before labeling type 2

stages.label: First steps and lifestyle
stages.question: What does everyone need from day one?
stages.decision: DSMES, nutrition therapy, activity, sleep, tobacco cessation, and an agreed weight goal

stages.label: First medicines
stages.question: Which medicine fits this person at the start?
stages.decision: Metformin and/or early SGLT2i or GLP-1-based therapy; insulin if glucose is very high

stages.label: Heart and kidney protection
stages.question: Is there ASCVD, heart failure, or CKD?
stages.decision: Add agents with proven benefit irrespective of A1C; consider layering SGLT2i + GLP-1-based therapy

stages.label: Adding and intensifying
stages.question: Not at goal — what next?
stages.decision: Intensify without delay: GLP-1-based therapy before insulin, then basal insulin, then mealtime insulin or surgery

stages.label: Long-term care and complications
stages.question: What has to happen every year?
stages.decision: Eyes, feet, kidneys, lipids, blood pressure, mood, and vaccines on schedule

Patient basics.label: age
Patient basics.help: Adult guide only. Age shapes goals (e.g., CGM time <70 mg/dL goal <1% for older adults vs <4% for most, ADA 6.3c) and the prevention-metformin signal (strongest in ages 25–59 in DPP, ADA 3.7).
Patient basics.helpPatient: Your age helps set goals that are safe for you.

Patient basics.label: BMI
Patient basics.help: Weight-lowering agents are preferred with overweight/obesity (ADA/EASD 2026). Metabolic surgery could be considered at BMI ≥30 (≥27.5 Asian ancestry) and should be considered at ≥35 (≥32.5).
Patient basics.helpPatient: Body size helps decide whether weight-focused treatments make sense.

Patient basics.label: cost or access worry
Patient basics.help: ADA 9.5 lists cost and access as a named factor in drug choice; a yes flags lower-cost generics (metformin, sulfonylureas, pioglitazone, human insulin) and benefit programs — it never hides an option.
Patient basics.helpPatient: Tell your team if paying for medicines is hard. There are lower-cost choices.

Glucose and kidney labs.label: A1C
Glucose and kidney labs.help: Diagnosis ≥6.5%; prediabetes 5.7–6.4% (ADA Table 2.1/2.2). Goal <7% for many adults (ADA 6.3a). Insulin should be considered when A1C >10% or glucose ≥300 mg/dL or symptoms (ADA 9.20).
Glucose and kidney labs.helpPatient: A1C shows your average blood sugar over about 3 months.

Glucose and kidney labs.label: eGFR
Glucose and kidney labs.help: Hard gates: metformin contraindicated <30; SGLT2 inhibitors start at ≥20 (glucose effect minimal <45) (ADA Table 9.2, 11.7a).
Glucose and kidney labs.helpPatient: A kidney filter number. Some medicines need a minimum level.

Glucose and kidney labs.label: urine albumin (UACR)
Glucose and kidney labs.help: Albuminuria (≥30 mg/g) marks CKD and drives kidney-protective therapy; nonsteroidal MRA when UACR >30 mg/g and eGFR >25 (ADA/EASD 2026). Check at least yearly (ADA 11.1a).
Glucose and kidney labs.helpPatient: A urine test for protein leaking from the kidneys.

Heart, kidney and safety.label: established ASCVD
Heart, kidney and safety.help: Heart attack, stroke, or arterial disease. Triggers GLP-1 RA and/or SGLT2i with proven CV benefit irrespective of A1C (ADA 9.7).
Heart, kidney and safety.helpPatient: Have you had a heart attack, stroke, or blocked arteries?

Heart, kidney and safety.label: heart failure
Heart, kidney and safety.help: HFrEF or HFpEF: SGLT2i recommended irrespective of A1C (ADA 9.8); pioglitazone should not be used (ADA Table 9.2).
Heart, kidney and safety.helpPatient: Has a doctor told you your heart is weak or stiff (heart failure)?

Heart, kidney and safety.label: chronic kidney disease
Heart, kidney and safety.help: CKD (eGFR 20–60 and/or albuminuria): SGLT2i or GLP-1 RA with proven kidney benefit (ADA 9.10, 11.7).
Heart, kidney and safety.helpPatient: Have you been told your kidneys are not working fully?

Heart, kidney and safety.label: hypoglycemia risk
Heart, kidney and safety.help: High = e.g., prior severe or frequent lows, impaired hypoglycemia awareness, or treatment with insulin or a sulfonylurea. Weigh risk when choosing drugs and goals (ADA 6.13).
Heart, kidney and safety.helpPatient: How likely you are to have low blood sugar episodes.

Heart, kidney and safety.label: personal/family medullary thyroid cancer or MEN2
Heart, kidney and safety.help: Hard gate: GLP-1-based therapies (except lixisenatide and twice-daily exenatide) are contraindicated (ADA/EASD 2026).
Heart, kidney and safety.helpPatient: A rare thyroid cancer or gene syndrome in you or your family. It rules out some shots.

Prevention & prediabetes.name: Diabetes prevention program (intensive lifestyle)
Prevention & prediabetes.guideline: ADA 2026 Rec 3.3/3.5 (A); USPSTF B (refer people with prediabetes to preventive interventions)
Prevention & prediabetes.patient: A year-long coached program to lose a little weight and move more. It roughly halved new diabetes in the big US study.

Prevention & prediabetes.name: Metformin for prevention
Prevention & prediabetes.guideline: ADA 2026 Rec 3.7 (A): consider in high-risk adults, especially ages 25–59 with BMI ≥35, FPG ≥110, A1C ≥6.0%, or prior gestational diabetes
Prevention & prediabetes.toxicity: GI upset (bloating, diarrhea); possible vitamin B12 lowering with long use

outcome.value: 31% lower over ~2.8 yr (DPP); less effective than lifestyle

Prevention & prediabetes.patient: A low-cost pill that lowers the chance of getting diabetes, though less than lifestyle changes do.

Newly diagnosed.name: Lifestyle foundation: MNT + DSMES + activity
Newly diagnosed.guideline: ADA 2026 Rec 5.1–5.2, 5.10, 5.36–5.37; ADA/EASD 2026: DSMES as important as drug choice
Newly diagnosed.toxicity: none specific; very-low-energy diets may need medicine adjustment to avoid hypoglycemia and ketoacidosis (ADA/EASD 2026)
Newly diagnosed.patient: Classes, a food plan, and regular activity. This is the base of every plan, with or without medicines.

Newly diagnosed.name: Intensive weight-loss program aiming at remission
Newly diagnosed.guideline: ADA/EASD 2026: consider intensive lifestyle therapy aiming for ≥10% weight loss with the possibility of remission
Newly diagnosed.toxicity: hunger, fatigue during low-energy diet; medicines may need adjusting to avoid lows

outcome.value: 46% vs 4% (DiRECT); 13% of continuing participants in remission at 5 yr (ADA/EASD 2026)

drugs: Total diet replacement then stepped food reintroduction
Newly diagnosed.patient: A structured diet program that put almost half of people into remission for a year. Keeping it off long-term is hard.

Newly diagnosed.name: Metformin
Newly diagnosed.guideline: ADA 2026: historically first-line; effective, safe, inexpensive (Sec. 9). ADA/EASD 2026: SGLT2i/GLP-1 benefits are independent of metformin
Newly diagnosed.toxicity: GI intolerance (reduce with slow titration, extended release, with food); vitamin B12 deficiency; contraindicated eGFR <30

outcome.value: 32% lower (UKPDS 34); MI and death benefit persisted at 10-yr follow-up (UKPDS 80)

Newly diagnosed.patient: A cheap pill used for decades. Stomach upset is common at first and usually settles.

Newly diagnosed.name: Early SGLT2 inhibitor (organ protection from diagnosis)
Newly diagnosed.guideline: ADA/EASD 2026: earlier use, potentially from diagnosis, of SGLT2i and/or GLP-1-based therapy; ADA 9.6 combination can be considered at start
Newly diagnosed.evidence: CVOT meta-evidence; absolute benefit smaller in low-risk people
Newly diagnosed.toxicity: genital yeast infections; rare DKA (incl. euglycemic); volume depletion
Newly diagnosed.patient: A daily pill that protects the heart and kidneys and lowers sugar a bit. Keep the genital area clean.

Newly diagnosed.name: Early GLP-1 receptor agonist
Newly diagnosed.guideline: ADA/EASD 2026: earlier GLP-1-based therapy, potentially from diagnosis; ADA 9.21 preferred to insulin when no severe hyperglycemia
Newly diagnosed.toxicity: nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation mainly during dose escalation; gallbladder events; retinopathy monitoring
Newly diagnosed.patient: A weekly or daily medicine that lowers sugar and weight. Nausea is common at first.

Newly diagnosed.name: Tirzepatide (dual GIP/GLP-1 RA)
Newly diagnosed.guideline: ADA 2026 Table 9.2: very high glucose-lowering efficacy, very high weight loss
Newly diagnosed.toxicity: GI effects as for GLP-1 RAs; more GI events than dulaglutide in SURPASS-CVOT

outcome.type: A1C change vs placebo at 40 wk

Newly diagnosed.patient: A weekly shot with the strongest sugar and weight lowering of the current options. Stomach side effects are common early.

Newly diagnosed.name: Insulin first when glucose is very high
Newly diagnosed.guideline: ADA 2026 Rec 9.20 (E): consider insulin with symptoms or A1C >10% / glucose ≥300 mg/dL
Newly diagnosed.patient: If sugar is very high, insulin can bring it down quickly. It may not be forever.

Heart or kidney disease present.name: SGLT2 inhibitor with proven CV benefit (ASCVD)
Heart or kidney disease present.toxicity: genital mycotic infection (more common in EMPA-REG); DKA rare (DECLARE 0.3% vs 0.1%)
Heart or kidney disease present.patient: A pill shown to cut heart attacks, strokes and heart deaths in people who already have heart disease.

Heart or kidney disease present.name: SGLT2 inhibitor for heart failure
Heart or kidney disease present.guideline: ADA 2026 Rec 9.8 (A): HFrEF or HFpEF, irrespective of A1C
Heart or kidney disease present.toxicity: volume depletion — review diuretics; genital infection; rare DKA

Heart or kidney disease present.name: SGLT2 inhibitor for CKD
Heart or kidney disease present.guideline: ADA 2026 Rec 11.7a (A): start at eGFR ≥20, continue until kidney failure; KDIGO 2022 aligned
Heart or kidney disease present.toxicity: early small eGFR dip; volume depletion; genital infection
Heart or kidney disease present.patient: Slows kidney damage and is worth taking even when sugar is already at goal.

Heart or kidney disease present.name: GLP-1 RA with proven CV benefit (ASCVD)
Heart or kidney disease present.guideline: ADA 2026 Rec 9.7 (A); ADA/EASD 2026: reduces MACE and all-cause mortality
Heart or kidney disease present.toxicity: GI effects; retinopathy complications higher with semaglutide in SUSTAIN-6 (HR 1.76)
Heart or kidney disease present.patient: A shot (or pill) shown to lower heart attacks and strokes in people with heart disease.

Heart or kidney disease present.name: Semaglutide for CKD
Heart or kidney disease present.guideline: ADA 2026 Rec 11.7b (A); ADA/EASD 2026: semaglutide indicated to reduce CKD progression
Heart or kidney disease present.toxicity: GI effects; monitor kidney function if severe GI losses
Heart or kidney disease present.patient: A weekly shot that slowed kidney disease in a large trial.

Heart or kidney disease present.name: Tirzepatide with ASCVD
Heart or kidney disease present.guideline: FDA label (DailyMed, effective 2026-11-16): indicated to reduce the risk of MACE (CV death, non-fatal MI, non-fatal stroke) in adults with T2D at high risk; ADA/EASD 2026 consensus
Heart or kidney disease present.toxicity: more GI adverse events than dulaglutide; similar serious adverse events
Heart or kidney disease present.patient: At least as protective for the heart as an older proven shot, with more weight loss.

Heart or kidney disease present.name: SGLT2i + GLP-1-based combination
Heart or kidney disease present.guideline: ADA/EASD 2026: combination could be considered with high CV risk, CVD or kidney disease irrespective of A1C; early combination with concomitant CVD, CKD and HF
Heart or kidney disease present.toxicity: sum of both classes; volume depletion with GI losses
Heart or kidney disease present.patient: Using both protective medicines together when heart or kidney risk is high.

Heart or kidney disease present.name: Nonsteroidal MRA (finerenone) for albuminuric CKD
Heart or kidney disease present.guideline: ADA/EASD 2026: recommended with albuminuria when eGFR >25; with UACR >30 mg/g
Heart or kidney disease present.evidence: phase 3 RCTs (FIDELIO-DKD, FIGARO-DKD) + prespecified pooled analysis (FIDELITY)
Heart or kidney disease present.toxicity: hyperkalemia — discontinuation for hyperkalemia 1.7% vs 0.6% (FIDELITY); check potassium

outcome.value: kidney composite 0.82 (FIDELIO-DKD); CV composite 0.87 (FIGARO-DKD); pooled CV 0.86 and kidney 0.77 (FIDELITY)

Heart or kidney disease present.patient: A kidney-protecting pill for people with protein in the urine. Potassium needs checking.

Needs more lowering.name: Add or switch to GLP-1-based therapy before insulin
Needs more lowering.guideline: ADA 2026 Rec 9.21 (A): GLP-1-based therapy preferred to insulin without severe hyperglycemia; Rec 9.15: do not delay intensification
Needs more lowering.toxicity: GI effects; do not combine with DPP-4i (Rec 9.18)

outcome.type: A1C change, tirzepatide vs semaglutide 1 mg

Needs more lowering.patient: If you are not at goal, a weekly shot is usually tried before insulin.

Needs more lowering.name: DPP-4 inhibitor
Needs more lowering.guideline: ADA 2026 Table 9.2: intermediate efficacy, weight neutral, CV neutral
Needs more lowering.evidence: CVOTs showed safety without CV benefit (per ADA/EASD 2026)
Needs more lowering.toxicity: low hypoglycemia; pancreatitis reported; joint pain; bullous pemphigoid; gallbladder signal; saxagliptin HF risk
Needs more lowering.patient: A gentle pill with few side effects but no heart or kidney protection.

Needs more lowering.name: Sulfonylurea
Needs more lowering.guideline: ADA 2026 Table 9.2: high efficacy, hypoglycemia risk, weight gain
Needs more lowering.toxicity: hypoglycemia; weight gain; less durable; glyburide not recommended in CKD

outcome.type: microvascular endpoints (SU or insulin vs conventional)

Needs more lowering.patient: A cheap, strong pill, but it can cause low blood sugar and some weight gain.

Needs more lowering.name: Pioglitazone
Needs more lowering.guideline: ADA 2026 Table 9.2: high efficacy, durable; Rec 9.13 option for MASH
Needs more lowering.toxicity: fluid retention and heart failure; weight gain; bone fracture; possible bladder cancer risk
Needs more lowering.patient: A low-cost pill that also helps fatty liver, but can cause swelling and weight gain. Not for heart failure.

Needs more lowering.name: Basal insulin
Needs more lowering.guideline: ADA 2026 Sec. 9 / Rec 9.22–9.23; ADA/EASD 2026: start as basal only, usually after GLP-1-based therapy; keep cardio-kidney agents
Needs more lowering.toxicity: hypoglycemia; weight gain; analogs less nocturnal hypoglycemia than NPH
Needs more lowering.patient: One shot a day of long-acting insulin, adjusted step by step. Glucagon and a low-sugar plan come with it.

Needs more lowering.name: Insulin intensification (mealtime or premixed)
Needs more lowering.guideline: ADA/EASD 2026: rapid- or ultrarapid-acting insulin can be added to basal for prandial glucose; premixed is convenient but less flexible
Needs more lowering.toxicity: highest hypoglycemia risk; weight gain; CGM recommended (ADA 7.15)
Needs more lowering.patient: Extra insulin at meals when long-acting insulin alone is not enough. A sensor (CGM) helps keep this safe.

Needs more lowering.name: Metabolic surgery
Needs more lowering.guideline: ADA/EASD 2026: could be considered BMI ≥30 (≥27.5 Asian ancestry); should be considered BMI ≥35 (≥32.5)
Needs more lowering.toxicity: surgical risk; anemia, fractures and GI adverse events more common after surgery (ARMMS-T2D); nutritional deficiencies; lean-mass loss — protein and resistance exercise advised

outcome.value: 37.5% vs 2.6% at 3 yr; 18.2% vs 6.2% at 7 yr; 12.7% vs 0% at 12 yr (ARMMS-T2D)

Needs more lowering.patient: Weight-loss surgery can put diabetes into remission for some people. It is a big step with lifelong follow-up.

milestones.title: First A1C recheck
milestones.window: ~3 months after diagnosis or any treatment change
review: CGM time in range / time below range if used
side effects and medication-taking (GI effects, genital infections)
hypoglycemia events if on insulin or sulfonylurea
intensify now if not at goal (do not delay)

milestones.title: Medication plan review
review: is an organ-protective agent indicated (new ASCVD, HF, CKD)?
cost and access barriers or rationing
reduce sulfonylurea/insulin when adding a new agent
DPP-4i should not be combined with GLP-1-based therapy

milestones.title: Annual complications review
review: dilated eye exam (or every 1–2 years if normal and at goal)

milestones.title: Insulin start and titration check
milestones.window: first weeks after insulin start, then each dose change
review: keep SGLT2i / GLP-1-based therapy unless not tolerated
hypoglycemia awareness screen at least yearly

milestones.title: CKD monitoring
milestones.window: 1–4 times per year depending on stage
review: potassium if on ACEi/ARB, diuretic, or finerenone

milestones.title: Long-term metformin check
milestones.trigger: metformin use for >5 years, or anemia / neuropathy

honesty: Every number shown comes from a listed trial or guideline; if a source does not state it, the guide leaves it out.
Relative benefits from high-risk outcome trials are not shown as if they apply equally to low-risk people; ADA/EASD 2026 notes absolute benefit is smaller when baseline risk is low.
Trial populations are named: SELECT enrolled people WITHOUT diabetes and is not presented as a diabetes trial result.
Noninferior is not called superior: SURPASS-CVOT met noninferiority vs dulaglutide, not superiority.
Harms stay visible: ACCORD showed higher mortality with near-normal A1C targets using high-hypoglycemia drugs, and Look AHEAD did not reduce cardiovascular events.
Registry statuses carry the date they were checked; results not yet peer-reviewed are marked unverified.
Low-cost options (metformin, sulfonylureas, pioglitazone, human insulin) are always shown, not hidden behind newer drugs.
If this guide disagrees with the current ADA Standards or your clinician, trust them; the 2027 Standards are expected in December 2026.
gates: Diagnosis needs two abnormal results (same or different tests) unless there is unequivocal hyperglycemia with symptoms or crisis
Features suggesting type 1 diabetes (age <35, BMI <25, weight loss, ketoacidosis, glucose >360 mg/dL) route away from this pathway
Metformin: contraindicated at eGFR <30; consider dose reduction at eGFR <45; eGFR 30–45 carries risk of dips below 30
SGLT2 inhibitors: initiate only at eGFR ≥20; glucose-lowering effect minimal below 45 but kidney/heart benefit continues
SGLT2 inhibitors: DKA risk (including euglycemic) — sick-day plan; stop 3–4 days before scheduled surgery, in critical illness or prolonged fasting
GLP-1 RAs and tirzepatide: contraindicated with personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer or MEN2
GLP-1-based therapy: not recommended with gastroparesis; do not start if high pancreatitis risk; guidance before procedures (aspiration risk); monitor retinopathy
Sulfonylureas and insulin: hypoglycemia risk — reduce or reassess their dose when adding another glucose-lowering agent; prescribe glucagon with insulin
Pioglitazone: do not use in heart failure; caution with prior bladder cancer, avoid with active bladder cancer
Do not combine a DPP-4 inhibitor with a GLP-1 RA or tirzepatide
Insulin should be considered when A1C >10%, glucose ≥300 mg/dL, or symptomatic hyperglycemia, regardless of other therapy
Women of reproductive potential: contraception counseling before medicines not approved in pregnancy
care: Primary care team (physician, NP/PA, pharmacist) as the home base
Behavioral health professional when screening is positive
Endocrinology, cardiology, nephrology, or metabolic surgery when indicated

todo.title: Confirm the diagnosis
how: Ask which test came back high: A1C, fasting glucose, a glucose tolerance test, or a random glucose with symptoms.
Unless your glucose was very high with symptoms, have the confirming test your team orders: the same test repeated, or a different one.
Ask whether type 1 diabetes needs to be ruled out (for example with younger age, low weight, weight loss, or ketones).
avoid: Don't start home remedies or supplements instead of confirming.
Don't panic over a single borderline number. Repeat testing is normal.
todo.details: Diabetes is diagnosed with an A1C of 6.5% or higher, a fasting glucose of 126 mg/dL or higher, a 2-hour glucose tolerance result of 200 mg/dL or higher, or a random glucose of 200 mg/dL or higher with classic symptoms. Without clear-cut high sugar, two abnormal results are needed. They can come from two tests on the same day or the same test on two days.

todo.title: Book your first full visit and baseline tests
todo.timing: Book this week; the visit within the first month
how: Ask for a longer first visit to go over your history, medicines and goals.
Bring a list of every medicine and supplement you take, and your vaccine records.
Ask for the baseline tests: A1C, cholesterol (lipid panel), liver tests, kidney tests (eGFR and the urine albumin test, UACR), and a blood count.
Ask which vaccines you are due for.
avoid: Don't skip the urine albumin test. eGFR alone misses early kidney damage.
Don't assume your vaccines are up to date. Bring your records.
todo.details: The ADA lists these tests for the first visit, and most are repeated at least once a year. Vaccines to review include yearly flu, COVID-19, pneumococcal, hepatitis B (under 60), and age-based zoster, RSV and Tdap.

alerts.label: Book first full diabetes visit and baseline labs (A1C, lipids, liver, eGFR, UACR, CBC)

todo.title: Start your medicines safely
todo.timing: From the day they are prescribed
how: Ask what each medicine is for: sugar, heart, kidney or weight.
Metformin: take it with food. The dose is raised slowly, and the extended-release form can ease stomach upset.
GLP-1 or tirzepatide shots: eat smaller meals and stop when you feel full.
SGLT2 pills: keep the genital area clean, and learn the warning signs of ketoacidosis (see Good to know).
If cost is a problem, tell your team. Lower-cost options exist.
avoid: Don't stop a medicine on your own because of mild early side effects. Call first.
Don't double up on a missed dose without advice.
On an SGLT2 pill, don't assume a normal glucose reading rules out ketoacidosis.
todo.details: Many people now start an SGLT2 inhibitor or a GLP-1-based medicine early, sometimes from diagnosis, alongside or instead of metformin. Nausea on GLP-1 medicines usually eases after dose increases. Ketoacidosis is a rare but serious side effect of SGLT2 pills, and glucose can be normal when it happens. Its signs are nausea, vomiting, belly pain, tiredness and labored breathing. If they occur, stop the medicine and get medical help right away. Your team may ask you to check ketones.

alerts.label: Take diabetes medicines as prescribed

todo.title: Quit tobacco and vaping
todo.who: Primary care, quit line or cessation program
how: Tell your team about any tobacco or vape use.
Ask for both counseling and a quit medicine. Using them together works best.
Set a quit date and remove triggers at home.
avoid: Don't switch to e-cigarettes as a 'safe' option. Avoiding them completely is advised.
Don't give up after a slip. Restart the plan.
todo.details: The ADA advises avoiding all tobacco and vaping. For people who use them, it recommends counseling plus medicine to quit. Quitting also helps protect the kidneys and feet.

alerts.label: Tobacco/vaping: ask your team about counseling plus quit medicine
Raise tobacco/vaping status at your diabetes visit

todo.title: Join a diabetes education program (DSMES)
how: Ask for a referral to diabetes self-management education and support (DSMES).
Choose group, one-on-one or telehealth. All of them count.
avoid: Don't treat education as optional. It matters as much as the choice of medicine.
Don't wait until problems start.
todo.details: DSMES teaches the daily skills of diabetes: food, activity, medicines, monitoring, and problem-solving. The ADA advises it at diagnosis, every year, when goals are not met, when new problems develop, and at life transitions. The ADA/EASD 2026 report calls it as important as medicine selection.

alerts.label: Ask for a DSMES (diabetes education) referral

todo.title: Set up glucose checks
how: Ask whether you need a glucose meter or a continuous glucose monitor (CGM).
Ask what your targets are. Many adults using a CGM aim for more than 70% of the time in range.
Check as often as your plan says, and bring the readings to every visit.
avoid: Don't change your medicine doses based on readings without talking to your team.
todo.details: A CGM is recommended for people on insulin, and for people on medicines that can cause lows. Metformin, SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1-based medicines and DPP-4 inhibitors rarely cause lows by themselves; insulin and sulfonylureas can. If you take one of those, also do the step "If you take insulin or a sulfonylurea: be ready for lows".

alerts.label: Check glucose / review CGM as your plan says

todo.title: See a dietitian and build your plate
todo.timing: Within the first month; review every 6 months
how: Ask for medical nutrition therapy with a registered dietitian.
Use the plate method: half non-starchy vegetables, a quarter protein, a quarter carbohydrates.
Choose vegetables, whole fruit, legumes, whole grains, nuts and lean protein.
Agree on a weight goal with your team.
avoid: Don't drink sugar-sweetened drinks.
Don't start a crash diet without telling your team; medicines may need adjusting.
Don't chase one 'perfect' diet. Several eating patterns work.
todo.details: There is no single best split of carbohydrate, protein and fat; the best plan is one you can keep up. Losing at least 5% of body weight improves glucose, cholesterol and blood pressure, and 10% or more may bring remission. On a weight-lowering medicine or after surgery, get enough protein and do strength exercise to protect muscle.

alerts.label: Book a registered dietitian (medical nutrition therapy) visit
Review eating plan and weight goal with your team

todo.title: Protect your heart: blood pressure and cholesterol
how: Ask what your blood pressure goal is (below 130/80 for most people, if it can be reached safely).
Ask whether you should take a statin for cholesterol.
If you have heart disease, ask about your LDL cholesterol goal and about aspirin.
If you have high blood pressure, learn to measure it at home.
avoid: Don't stop a statin for vague aches without talking to your team.
Don't focus only on sugar. Protecting your heart matters as much.
todo.details: Heart disease is the main long-term danger in type 2 diabetes. Lowering blood pressure and LDL cholesterol reduces heart attacks, strokes, and eye and kidney damage. A moderate-intensity statin is advised for ages 40–75 without heart disease, and a high-intensity one when risk is higher; with heart disease the LDL goal is below 55 mg/dL. Blood pressure should be measured at every routine visit, or at least every 6 months. Some diabetes medicines (SGLT2 and GLP-1) also protect the heart.

alerts.label: Blood pressure check (every routine visit, at least every 6 months)
Home blood pressure reading (if you have hypertension)

todo.title: Get a dilated eye exam
how: Book a dilated eye exam with an ophthalmologist or optometrist.
If you start semaglutide or another GLP-1 medicine, tell your eye doctor.
avoid: Don't wait for blurry vision. Early eye damage has no symptoms.
todo.details: Type 2 diabetes can damage the eyes before it is diagnosed, which is why the first exam happens at diagnosis. After that it is yearly; if exams are normal and glucose is at goal, your eye doctor may stretch it to every 1–2 years. Retinopathy should be monitored on GLP-1 medicines.

alerts.label: Book dilated eye exam (due at diagnosis)
Reminder: dilated eye exam done this month?

todo.title: See a dentist
todo.timing: Within the first month; then regularly
how: Book a dental and gum (periodontal) check-up.
Tell the dentist you have diabetes.
avoid: Don't ignore bleeding gums.
todo.details: Gum disease is more common with diabetes and is linked to a higher A1C. Treating it may improve glucose.

alerts.label: Dental and gum check-up

todo.title: Make a written sick-day plan
how: Get a written plan that says which medicines to keep, pause or adjust when you are sick or cannot eat.
When sick: check your glucose about every 4 hours and drink plenty of fluids.
If you cannot eat normally: take about 50 g of carbohydrate every 4 hours (for example juice or applesauce).
Keep the plan where you and your family can find it.
avoid: Don't stop insulin on your own when you are sick.
Don't keep taking an SGLT2 pill through vomiting or fasting unless you've been told to.
Don't wait if you feel confused. Have someone call for help.
todo.details: Illness can push glucose up and cause dehydration, and SGLT2 pills carry a rare risk of ketoacidosis even with normal glucose, so they are often paused when you are sick. Go to the emergency room for vomiting or diarrhea lasting over 6 hours, being unable to keep liquids down for 4 hours, ketones, trouble breathing, or glucose below 60 mg/dL.

alerts.label: Make or update your written sick-day plan with your team

todo.title: Check your feet every day
todo.who: You; podiatry if there is a problem
how: Look at and feel your feet every day for cuts, blisters, redness or calluses. Use a mirror if needed.
Wash your feet daily and dry carefully between the toes.
Moisturize dry skin and cut toenails straight across.
Check inside your shoes before putting them on, and wear well-fitting shoes.
If you find a sore or a spot that looks like one is starting, contact a foot-care professional quickly.
avoid: Don’t walk barefoot, in socks without shoes, or in thin-soled slippers, indoors or outdoors.
Don't use chemical products or plasters to remove calluses.
Avoid tight socks and very hot or very cold exposure.
Don't skip a day because your feet feel fine. Nerve damage can hide injuries.
todo.details: Check your feet every day by touch or with an unbreakable mirror, and have a professional exam at least once a year. The International Working Group on the Diabetic Foot (IWGDF) gives these self-care steps for people at increased foot risk, which is anyone with lost feeling, poor circulation, or a past ulcer. The ADA advises foot self-care education and daily self-checks for everyone with diabetes.

alerts.label: Daily foot check (look and feel; use a mirror)

todo.title: Move more: 150 minutes a week, plus strength
how: Build up to 150 minutes or more a week of moderate activity, such as brisk walking, over at least 3 days.
Spread it out so you are never more than 2 days in a row without activity.
Add strength exercise 2–3 times a week, on days that are not back to back.
Break up sitting at least every 30 minutes with a short stand or walk.
If you take insulin or a sulfonylurea, agree an exercise plan with your team first (see the lows step).
avoid: Don't jump straight to hard workouts. Build up gradually, keeping your other conditions in mind.
Don't sit for hours at a time. Short movement breaks count.
todo.details: The ADA/EASD "five S" approach is standing, stepping, sweating (aerobic), strengthening and sleep. More activity brings more benefit, so increase it gradually when it is safe. On insulin or a sulfonylurea, activity can cause lows, even several hours later: you may need carbohydrate first if your glucose is below 90 mg/dL, and should check before, during and after exercise.

alerts.label: Plan this week: 150+ min aerobic over 3+ days, plus 2–3 strength sessions
Movement break: stand or walk briefly (break up sitting at least every 30 min)

todo.title: Sleep and stress
how: Keep a regular sleep routine.
Tell your team about snoring, daytime sleepiness or poor sleep.
Ask for a behavioral health referral if worry about diabetes or about lows is wearing you down.
avoid: Don't hide burnout or low mood. It is common and treatable.
Don't assume tiredness is 'just diabetes'.
todo.details: Diabetes distress is the emotional strain of daily self-care. It is different from depression and is linked to glucose levels. Sleep apnea screening is part of the diabetes evaluation.

alerts.label: Wind down for a regular bedtime

todo.title: Recheck your A1C and adjust the plan
todo.timing: About 3 months after starting; then every 3–6 months
how: Book the follow-up A1C before you leave your first visit.
Bring your glucose or CGM readings, any side effects, and your questions.
Review every medicine with your team at this visit.
If you are not at goal, expect the plan to change now rather than "wait and see".
avoid: Don't skip the recheck because you feel fine.
Don't stay above goal for months without a change.
todo.details: A1C reflects about 3 months of glucose, so this is the first fair look at whether the plan works. The ADA advises an A1C every 3 months when you are not at goal or after a change, and at least twice a year once you are at goal and stable. Your medicine plan should be reviewed every 3–6 months. Any serious low (below 54 mg/dL, or needing help) should prompt a review.

alerts.label: A1C recheck (every 3 months until at goal; then at least twice a year)
Medication plan review with your team (ADA: every 3–6 months)

todo.title: Your yearly check-up list
how: Kidney tests: the urine albumin test (UACR) and eGFR.
A full foot exam, including the monofilament test for lost feeling.
A dilated eye exam (your eye doctor may stretch this to every 1–2 years if exams are normal).
A screen for diabetes distress, depression and anxiety.
A flu vaccine, and a check of your other vaccines.
A diabetes education (DSMES) refresher, and a review of your sick-day plan.
If you have taken metformin for more than 5 years: a vitamin B12 check.
avoid: Don't skip yearly checks because you feel fine. Kidney, eye and nerve damage start without symptoms.
todo.details: These are the checks the ADA advises at least once a year for everyone with type 2 diabetes. Set the reminders here so each one comes around on time.

alerts.label: Yearly kidney check: urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) and eGFR
Yearly professional foot exam with monofilament test
Yearly dilated eye exam (your eye doctor may extend to every 1–2 years if normal)
Yearly screen: diabetes distress, depression, anxiety
Yearly flu vaccine
Yearly DSMES refresher
Yearly sick-day plan review
Metformin 5+ years: ask about a vitamin B12 check

todo.phase: Only if this applies to you
todo.title: If you take insulin or a sulfonylurea: be ready for lows
todo.timing: Before your first dose; review every year
how: Learn the 15-15 rule: if glucose is below 70 mg/dL and you are awake, take 15 g of glucose (tablets or gel), recheck in 15 minutes, and repeat if still low.
Once you are back in range, eat something, because the medicine can cause another low.
Carry glucose tablets or gel, and keep some in your first-aid kit.
Get glucagon prescribed (ready-to-use forms are preferred), and show family where it is and how to give it.
Check your glucose before driving, and before and after drinking alcohol.
avoid: Don't drive while your glucose is low.
Don't use foods high in fat or protein to treat a low. They slow the rise.
Don't give food or drink to someone who isn't alert. That is when glucagon is used.
todo.details: A low is glucose under 70 mg/dL; under 54 mg/dL is serious, and needing someone else's help is the most serious level. Shakiness, sweating, hunger, confusion and a fast heartbeat are common signs. Alcohol can cause delayed lows on these medicines. Any serious low should prompt a review of your treatment plan, and structured education on lows is recommended for everyone taking insulin.

alerts.label: Check: glucose tablets in bag and glucagon not expired
Yearly hypoglycemia education and awareness review

todo.phase: Only if this applies to you
todo.title: If you could become pregnant: plan ahead
todo.who: Primary care, endocrinology, maternal-fetal medicine, diabetes educator
how: Use effective contraception (consider long-acting reversible methods) until your team says your plan and A1C are ready for pregnancy.
Before trying to conceive, work toward an A1C as close to normal as is safe, ideally below 6.5%.
Review every medicine with your team before conception.
Start a prenatal vitamin with 400–800 µg folic acid and 150 µg potassium iodide before conception.
Get a dilated eye exam before pregnancy and again in the first trimester.
avoid: Don't stop contraception before your team says you're ready.
Don't stay on a GLP-1 medicine, tirzepatide, an ACE inhibitor or an ARB if pregnancy is possible without effective contraception.
todo.details: High glucose around conception raises the risk of birth defects, preeclampsia and preterm birth, and planned care before pregnancy lowers these risks. GLP-1 medicines and tirzepatide should be stopped before pregnancy (the semaglutide label says at least 2 months ahead). ACE inhibitors, ARBs and MRAs should be stopped before conception, and most cholesterol medicines, including statins, usually are too. Insulin is the preferred glucose-lowering medicine during pregnancy.

alerts.label: Discuss pregnancy plans and contraception with your team
Yearly family-planning and medication review

todo.phase: Only if this applies to you
todo.title: If you are having surgery or a procedure
todo.timing: As soon as it is planned
how: Tell the team doing the procedure about every diabetes medicine you take.
Ask your team for the exact dates to stop and restart an SGLT2 pill.
If you take a GLP-1 medicine or tirzepatide, ask for a personal plan for holding it.
For a planned operation, aim to have your A1C below 8% in the 3 months before.
avoid: Don't decide on your own how long to hold a weekly GLP-1 shot.
Don't restart an SGLT2 pill while you are still unwell or not eating.
Don't wait until the day of surgery to mention these medicines.
todo.details: SGLT2 inhibitors are usually stopped 3 days before scheduled surgery (4 days for ertugliflozin) and restarted only when you are eating and well. GLP-1 medicines and tirzepatide carry an FDA label warning about aspiration (food entering the lungs) under anesthesia or deep sedation, so the holding plan is individualized. Glucose around surgery is usually kept between 100 and 180 mg/dL.

alerts.label: Procedure planned? Tell your team about SGLT2 and GLP-1 medicines now

todo.phase: Only if this applies to you
todo.title: If you are 65 or older: review your goals every year
how: Ask for a yearly check of falls, memory, mood, pain, continence, frailty, lows and how many medicines you take.
Agree on personal goals with your team.
If you are on insulin, ask about a continuous glucose monitor (CGM).
Ask whether any medicine that causes lows can be reduced, switched or simplified.
avoid: Don't push for very tight numbers if they cause lows.
Don't keep a complicated insulin plan without asking whether it can be simplified.
todo.details: Older adults have a higher risk of lows, especially on insulin or sulfonylureas. Typical goals are an A1C below 7.0–7.5% if healthy, or below 8.0% with complex health or frailty. A blood pressure goal below 130/80 fits most older adults, with a more relaxed target, such as below 140/90, for people in poor health.

alerts.label: Yearly older-adult review: falls, memory, mood, lows, medicine count
